summary: Caris Life Sciences presented RNA sequencing of about 698,000 tumors, finding new drug-targetable gene fusions; no effect sizes were reported.
With FDA oversight of lab-developed tests struck down in March 2025, the fight is now over Medicare lab payment rates and modernized lab rules.
AI dominated the program; one plenary AI model classified brain tumors with 97% accuracy, beating all eight neuropathologists.
Cheap blood-based cancer testing, framed as a possible $100 liquid biopsy, was a leading theme; few companies announced dollar-figure news.

items.title: Whole transcriptome sequencing (WTS) of tumors for gene fusions, Caris Life Sciences
lines: Caris presented two studies; one analyzed whole-transcriptome RNA (ribonucleic acid) sequencing across 698,406 solid tumors profiled from 2019 to 2026.
It found new actionable gene fusions with outcomes said to be comparable to known partners; hazard ratios and p-values were not reported.
Older targeted tests risked missing new fusions, especially in sarcomas and central nervous system tumors; figures not reported.
Investor read: real-world data from about 700,000 transcriptomes supports Caris pitching its data to drug developers; revenue figures not reported.

items.title: Lab regulation and Medicare payment policy, Association for Molecular Pathology (AMP) advocacy
lines: The FDA (Food and Drug Administration) rule on laboratory-developed tests (LDTs) was vacated nationwide on March 31, 2025, in AMP v. FDA; FDA did not appeal.
AMP members lobbied more than 30 congressional offices for the RESULTS Act, which would reform how Medicare sets Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule (CLFS) rates.

CMS (Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services) issued a July 2026 Request for Information on modernizing Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments (CLIA) rules; AMP responded. Proposed rule dates not reported.
No new fee-schedule rate cuts or dollar figures were reported from the meeting itself; figures not reported.

items.title: Artificial intelligence (AI) in molecular diagnostics, AMP press program (ALMA Genomics, private; academic groups)
lines: ALMA 3, an AI model trained on over 110,000 samples, detected blood cancers with 99.5% sensitivity and 90.9% positive predictive value across 81 subtypes.
University of Michigan's TPO-Agent (Turnkey Precision Oncology): about 95% of AI claims backed by cited evidence, vs 65% for a standard AI approach; 50 alterations, 10 patients.
Memorial Sloan Kettering (MSK): AI slide triage would have deferred rapid EGFR (epidermal growth factor receptor) testing in 26 of 80 lung cancers (33%), missing no EGFR-positive cases.
Mayo Clinic plenary: AI brain-tumor classification reached 97% accuracy, beating all 8 neuropathologists it was compared with.

items.title: Fragmentomics and the low-cost liquid biopsy (blood test for tumor DNA)
lines: Trade press called fragmentomics one of the buzziest terms at AMP 2026 and asked whether a $100 liquid biopsy has arrived.
McGill University data on esophageal adenocarcinoma: plasma separated cancer from non-cancer, and urine and vaginal swabs graded precancer; figures not reported.
Driver is ever-cheaper sequencing; which companies win the $100 test was not settled; figures not reported.

items.title: Booth showcase: MiSeq i100, TruSight Oncology Comprehensive, Pillar oncoReveal, BioInsight (Illumina)
lines: Illumina featured MiSeq i100 sequencer and an in vitro diagnostic (IVD) corner with FDA-approved TruSight Oncology Comprehensive and Pillar oncoReveal; pricing and placements not reported.
Workshops on November 11 covered whole-genome sequencing, AI-assisted informatics and epigenomic profiling; figures not reported.

items.title: Tools vendors: Thermo Fisher, Roche, Danaher (IDT), Bionano, Oxford Nanopore
lines: Thermo Fisher (booth 709) workshop on alternative analytes when tumor tissue is limited for next-generation sequencing (NGS); figures not reported.
Volta Labs (private) showed AXELIOS 1 library prep automated on Callisto in collaboration with Roche; trade press also headlined a Roche mesothelioma test launch; figures not reported.
Danaher's Integrated DNA Technologies (booth 1014) showed blood-cancer NGS workflows; Bionano (booth 825) showed optical genome mapping; figures not reported.
Oxford Nanopore hosted oncology and rare-disease workshops; figures not reported.

items.title: Rapid, decentralized testing: VedaBio CRISPR platform and Fapon enzymes (both private)
lines: VedaBio showed proof-of-concept sample-to-answer times under 10 minutes using CRISPR (clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats) detection that skips the amplification step.
Fapon's ProPrime II Taq enzyme runs four-target quantitative PCR (qPCR, quantitative polymerase chain reaction) in under 20 minutes; it works with 5% whole blood present.

expert_minds: AI performance vs human expertise: plenaries by Kenneth Aldape (Mayo Clinic) and Benjamin Solomon (NIH), per Inside Precision Medicine.
AI, regulation and labor shortages as threats to the field, per an Inside Precision Medicine headline about the AMP president; article not opened.
Fragmentomics and cheap multi-omic liquid biopsy, per Inside Precision Medicine wrap-up citing Hanlee Ji and Julia Burnier.
Payment reform (RESULTS Act) and CLIA modernization after the LDT court win, per AMP newsroom and committee reports.
